title: The Cold Email Setup Checklist: Domains, DNS Records and a Two-Week Warm-Up
description: The setup checklist from the reel: separate sending domains, SPF, DKIM and DMARC with example values, and a two-week warm-up plan.
lead: This is the full setup checklist from the reel. Before a single cold email goes out, three things must be in place: separate sending domains, the right DNS records and a two-week warm-up. Here's exactly how to do each one.
insider: This setup comes first on every client campaign we run. It's why one client could send **96,408 emails in 5 days with a 0.45% bounce rate and book 25 calls** that same week: the inboxes were warm and the foundation was ready on day one. The checklist is the easy part. Running and watching dozens of inboxes every day is the work we do for clients.

blocks.text: Why the foundation beats clever copy
The campaigns that win are rarely the ones with the cleverest copy. They're the ones whose emails actually reach the inbox. If your setup is weak, your best email lands in spam and nobody reads it.

[Google's sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126) require SPF or DKIM for every sender, and SPF, DKIM **and** DMARC for anyone sending 5,000+ messages a day to Gmail. Google also asks senders to keep spam rates under **0.3%** and to increase volume slowly.

**Why:** if a sending domain gets flagged, you swap it out. If your main domain gets flagged, your invoices, proposals and client emails start landing in spam too. Custom domains also do better than free addresses: [Hunter's 2026 report](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email) found **5.2% replies from custom domains vs 2.5%** from free addresses like Gmail.

items: Never send cold email from your main domain.
Buy lookalike domains. For acme.com: getacme.com, acmehq.com, tryacme.com.
Choose **.com** when you can.
Forward each lookalike domain to your real website.
Put **no more than 3 inboxes on each domain**, and keep 1 spare domain warming in the background.

blocks.text: **Why:** these records prove the email really comes from you and wasn't changed on the way. Set all three on every sending domain, before warm-up starts.

head: Record
What it does
Example (Google Workspace)
rows: Lists the servers allowed to send for your domain
A signature that proves the email wasn't changed
Generate the key in your email admin panel, then add it as a TXT record
Tells inboxes what to do when SPF or DKIM fails

items: Log in to your domain registrar's DNS settings.
Add the SPF record as a TXT record. Use only **one** SPF record per domain.
Generate DKIM in your email provider and add it. Google recommends a **2048-bit** key if your provider supports it.
Add the DMARC record. A policy of "none" is fine to start; Google allows it.
Check all three with a free DNS checker. Our [DNS records guide](/blog/dns-records-for-cold-email.html) walks through every value.

blocks.label: Using Microsoft 365 or another provider?
blocks.text: The SPF "include" part changes by provider. Copy it from your provider's own setup page, not from a random blog.

**Why:** a new inbox has no history. Google says to start with low volume and avoid sudden spikes. Warm-up tools like [Instantly](https://instantly.ai/email-warmup) send and receive normal-looking emails with other real inboxes, so providers learn your inbox is real.

items: Turn warm-up on for every new inbox on day 1.
Send **zero** cold emails for 14 days.
From day 15, start at about 10 cold emails per inbox per day.
Add 10 a week until you reach about 30. [Instantly's 2026 report](https://instantly.ai/cold-email-benchmark-report-2026) recommends building up over 4 to 6 weeks.
Keep warm-up on forever, even at full volume.

blocks.text: Worked example: setup for 400 emails a day

items: 400 ÷ 30 emails per inbox = 13.3, so round up to **14 inboxes**.
14 ÷ 3 inboxes per domain = 4.7, so round up to **5 domains** (room for 15 inboxes).
Add **1 spare domain** warming in the background.
Weeks 1–2: warm-up only. Week 3: 14 × 10 = 140 a day. Week 4: 14 × 20 = 280 a day. Week 5: 14 × 30 = **420 a day**, a little above the goal.

Move cold email to lookalike domains
Two SPF records on one domain

One bad day hurts all of them

items: Main domain never used for cold email
Lookalike .com domains bought and forwarded to the real website
Max 3 inboxes per domain, plus 1 spare domain
One SPF record per domain
DKIM key generated and added (2048-bit if possible)
DMARC record added (p=none is fine to start)
All records checked in a DNS checker
Google Postmaster Tools set up for each domain
14 days of warm-up before the first cold email
Ramp 10 → 20 → 30 per inbox per day, warm-up always on

blocks.label: AI prompt: plan your setup
blocks.text:
I want to send [number] cold emails a day. My main domain is [domain] and my email provider is [Google Workspace / Microsoft 365 / other].

1. Tell me how many inboxes and domains I need at 30 emails per inbox per day and max 3 inboxes per domain, plus 1 spare domain.
2. Suggest 8 lookalike .com domain ideas.
3. List the SPF, DKIM and DMARC records I need for my provider, and where to find the exact values.
4. Give me a week-by-week warm-up and ramp plan.

faq.q: How many domains do I need?
faq.a: Divide your daily goal by 30 to get inboxes, then divide by 3 to get domains. Round up both times and add 1 spare domain.

faq.q: Is DMARC with p=none good enough?
faq.a: Yes, to start. Google's guidelines say the DMARC policy can be set to none. What matters is that the record exists and SPF or DKIM passes.
A new inbox has no history. Two weeks of steady, normal activity gives providers a reason to trust it before cold email starts.
